title: Four central collective primitives
question: Which collective changes values, and which changes who holds them?
scope: Ranks are the four rows in each panel; tiles show logical ownership, not measured packet schedules.

steps.title: Aggregate and replicate
steps.description: AllReduce sums matching chunks over ranks and places every reduced chunk on every rank. Green tiles distinguish sums from original inputs.

steps.title: Concatenate without summing
steps.description: AllGather distributes each rank’s own chunk so every rank holds the concatenation. The bold outline traces chunk a through that ownership change.

steps.title: Aggregate into separate shards
steps.description: ReduceScatter computes the same per-chunk sums but leaves a different reduced shard on each rank. It does not replicate the complete result.

steps.title: Transpose destinations
steps.description: AllToAll routes each input chunk to its designated rank. Rank 0 receives the a chunks from every source; the values are rearranged rather than reduced.

title: Ring AllReduce data flow
question: Why does Ring AllReduce need two phases?
scope: The artwork shows four ranks and phase endpoints, with per-link step tiles; annotations do not interpolate unshown packet timings.

steps.title: Reduce separate chunks
steps.description: After three ReduceScatter steps, GPU 0 holds the complete sum of B while the other GPUs hold different complete sums. Gray partial tiles are not finished replicas.

steps.title: Close the logical ring
steps.description: The return link from GPU 3 to GPU 0 is part of every circulation round. The numbered tiles on links identify successive chunks, not simultaneous duplicate payloads.

steps.title: Distribute the finished sums
steps.description: Three further AllGather steps forward the completed shards without reducing them again. Every rank then holds the full sum.

title: Root Causes of Training Interruptions
question: Which interruptions dominate the reported training run, and what is unobserved?
scope: The bars count 419 recorded interruptions in one 54-day run, not universal fleet failure probabilities; silent corruption appears only when detected.

steps.title: Prioritize the frequent recorded causes
steps.description: The longest bars are faulty GPUs and GPU HBM3 memory. Their counts motivate recovery paths for frequent detectable accelerator failures.

steps.title: Include the rest of the system
steps.description: Software bugs and network switches or cables also interrupt the job. A GPU-only reliability model omits these operational paths.

steps.title: Do not read absence of detection as absence of corruption
steps.description: The silent-data-corruption bar includes six attributed interruptions. Uncaught corruption cannot appear in a root-cause count, so that small bar does not establish low total exposure.

title: Fail-stop vs. Byzantine failures
question: Why can a live worker still corrupt a distributed computation?
scope: The panels illustrate failure models; heartbeats establish liveness rather than numerical correctness.

steps.title: Detect an absent participant
steps.description: W2 stops sending heartbeats. The timeout converts missing progress into a suspicion of failure, with a delay chosen by the detector.

steps.title: Read the liveness result
steps.description: The fail-stop panel marks W2 unavailable while the other workers remain live. A timeout alone must still distinguish failure from slowness.

steps.title: Test values as well as presence
steps.description: W6 continues transmitting on schedule, so its liveness check stays green even after its gradients turn red. Correctness checks must cover the values used by the computation.

title: The ML failure spectrum
question: How should the fleet response change with fault persistence?
scope: Examples classify persistence, not a diagnosis from one failed attempt.

steps.title: Recover after a one-time event
steps.description: A transient fault appears once, then later attempts succeed. Retry or rollback repairs affected execution state when the fault leaves no lasting defect.

steps.title: Investigate faults that return under load
steps.description: The intermittent sequence fails again under load. Draining and stress-testing a suspect device addresses the recurring cause rather than repeatedly retrying production work.

steps.title: Replace a persistently faulty component
steps.description: The permanent sequence keeps failing on retries. Replacement and restoration are appropriate when the physical defect remains.

title: Silent data corruption propagation
question: Why can silent corruption make recent checkpoints unsafe?
scope: Time is explicitly not to scale; the causal chain illustrates possible propagation rather than the outcome of every bit flip.

origin.label: Bit flip and wrong tensor entry

steps.title: A valid-looking value changes
steps.description: A bit flip in memory or the ALU changes one tensor entry without necessarily stopping execution. A live process can therefore hold invalid numerical state.

steps.title: Training commits the error
steps.description: The backward pass can propagate corrupted values into gradients and weights. Future work then depends on state already affected by the fault.

steps.title: Contrast immediate detection
steps.description: A detected error traps and restarts from a checkpoint. Its recovery begins close to the fault rather than after extended training.

steps.title: Find the last trustworthy state
steps.description: The silent path saves corrupted state into later checkpoints before evaluation alerts. Rolling back requires a trustworthy earlier checkpoint, not simply the newest file.

title: Hot-spare failover
question: How does a hot-spare protocol preserve capacity while isolating a suspect GPU?
scope: The checker and replay identify a suspect, not a proof from one anomalous gradient; the sequence is a fleet protocol rather than full-step replication.

steps.title: Separate suspect from healthy participants
steps.description: The checker flags G2 while S is still an idle spare. Runtime evidence and replay guide which device should be isolated.

steps.title: Promote the standby into active work
steps.description: G2 leaves the active set and S takes its role. Spare capacity is consumed to keep productive execution going.

steps.title: Restore the reserve capacity
steps.description: A replacement S′ refills the spare position while G2 undergoes repair. The protocol must replenish the pool to handle another failure.

title: Error masking
question: Which fault effects does software-level injection omit?
scope: This is an abstraction boundary for experiments, not a probability tree; no branch frequencies are shown.

steps.title: Ask whether corrupted state is read
steps.description: A soft error can be masked before software sees it: an unused component, overwritten value, or squashed speculation may prevent propagation.

steps.title: Test the software-visible consequence
steps.description: If corrupted data is read, the effect can still be masked by a dead instruction, comparison, or uninfluential branch. Software fault injection starts below the first masking stage.

steps.title: Define the experiment’s coverage
steps.description: Only an unmasked effect reaches incorrect output or a crash in this diagram. Software-level injection cannot establish the hardware masking probability it bypasses.

title: The checkpoint trade-off
question: Why is neither constant saving nor very infrequent saving optimal?
scope: The curves use the chapter’s fixed first-order checkpoint model; they separate write overhead from expected rework and do not include every operational recovery cost.

steps.title: Avoid spending the run on writes
steps.description: The dashed blue save term rises sharply at short intervals because each write is repeated more often. Frequent checkpoints protect progress but consume productive time.

steps.title: Balance the two modeled costs
steps.description: At the marked optimum near fourteen minutes, the blue and red terms are equal and their black sum is minimized. The shallow floor means small interval errors have a modest cost.

steps.title: Account for work lost after a failure
steps.description: The dashed red expected-rework term grows as checkpoints spread apart. A long interval saves write overhead while exposing more unsaved computation.

title: Checkpoint-recovery timeline
question: Which parts of a failed run must be paid for again?
scope: The progress trace is schematic; save, rework, and recovery are distinct costs, not measured durations here.

steps.title: Make progress durable
steps.description: Green save segments persist a checkpoint. Work completed after that checkpoint is not yet protected by the next durable state.

steps.title: Lose unsaved work at failure
steps.description: The red extension in the progress trace rises past the last checkpoint, then drops back at failure. That interval is rework, not checkpoint-write overhead.

steps.title: Budget restart separately
steps.description: The recovery segment restores execution before useful computation resumes. A checkpoint policy must account for writes, lost work, and recovery time.

title: Distributed checkpoint architecture
question: Why can distributed checkpointing shorten the blocking write path?
scope: Background draining still consumes storage and network resources; local staging alone does not establish durable remote recovery.

drain.label: Concurrent blocking stage and background drain

steps.title: Locate centralized contention
steps.description: All workers send state through the coordinator before shared storage. The single ingress path can serialize checkpoint traffic.

steps.title: Stage each worker’s own shard
steps.description: The distributed design writes worker state directly to its local NVMe. Parallel writes reduce the blocking phase when the storage paths can sustain them.

steps.title: Track the remaining persistence work
steps.description: Dashed tails drain state to object storage after blocking staging. The recovery guarantee depends on where the needed checkpoint shards are durable when a failure occurs.

title: Elastic training recovery
question: What must change when a four-node training job resumes on three nodes?

steps.title: Begin with balanced ownership

steps.title: Pause to re-establish consistent state
steps.description: When N3 fails, the remaining nodes rendezvous and reload. Removing a node without coordinating membership, ranks, and data state is not sufficient.

steps.title: Resume with a new partition

title: Serving redundancy strategies
question: What resource is paid for before a replica fails?
scope: Weights remain resident in both schemes; the diagram compares allocation and traffic placement rather than a measured failover delay.

steps.title: Share requests among active replicas
steps.description: Active-active sends one-third of ingress traffic to each replica. All three hold weights and serve requests.

steps.title: Reserve room for redistribution
steps.description: Unused serving headroom allows survivors to absorb a failed replica’s share. Full normal utilization would remove this reserve.

steps.title: Pay for an idle but loaded standby
steps.description: Active-passive routes healthy traffic to the primary while the standby keeps weights loaded. The dashed path activates on failure, trading idle capacity for readiness.

title: The three pillars of observability
question: How do metrics, logs, and traces support one recovery decision?
scope: Correlated observations narrow causes; correlation by itself does not prove a physical or software root cause.

steps.title: Locate the symptom
steps.description: Metrics establish when and where the utilization pattern changed. They do not identify the exact operation that failed.

steps.title: Inspect the event and request path
steps.description: The log records an OOM exception while the trace locates a problematic service span. These streams answer different parts of the investigation.

steps.title: Join compatible evidence
steps.description: Request, trace, model, feature, and deployment identifiers connect events belonging to the same operating context. An unrelated log message is weaker evidence.

steps.title: Choose a bounded response
steps.description: The combined evidence can support shedding load, restarting, rolling back, or degrading service. Validate the result of the action rather than treating the correlation as proof.

title: Training failure signatures
question: What can a loss signature tell an operator before a diagnosis is confirmed?
scope: All four curves are synthetic examples. A transient rise or plateau is a symptom, not a unique diagnosis, and real healthy training need not decrease monotonically.

steps.title: Establish the expected trend
steps.description: The healthy panel supplies a declining but noisy reference. Monitoring should compare departures with the variation expected for the workload.

steps.title: Investigate a sharp spike
steps.description: The explosion panel highlights a short large increase before recovery. The signature narrows hypotheses but needs gradient and execution evidence before a cause is assigned.

steps.title: Detect lack of useful progress
steps.description: The plateau remains above the healthy reference. The shaded gap represents impaired optimization rather than a process that necessarily stopped running.

title: Weight Corruption via Bit Flip
question: How can one finite weight corruption affect multiple outputs?
scope: The shown bit flip is a specific FP32 example, not the expected effect of every random upset; output dominance depends on inputs and downstream computation.

flip.label: Bit 30 flip and extreme finite weight

steps.title: Locate the corrupted connection
steps.description: The red weight feeds hidden unit h2, whose outgoing edges reach both output logits. A single stored parameter can therefore influence more than one result.

steps.title: Read the original representation
steps.description: The upper bit field separates sign, eight exponent bits, and the mantissa. The stored weight is approximately 0.042 before corruption.

steps.title: Distinguish a large finite value from NaN
steps.description: Flipping the highlighted exponent bit scales the magnitude by 2^128 in this example. The resulting extreme value remains finite, so NaN and infinity checks alone need not catch it.

title: Silent Error Probability at Scale
question: How does a small per-device silent-error probability compound across a fleet?
scope: Each p is an illustrative independent residual-error probability over the same hour, not a measured hardware rate; corrected errors are excluded.

steps.title: Accumulate independent exposure
steps.description: The solid p=10^-3 curve rises with device count because the probability that every device avoids an event shrinks. The model computes one minus that no-event probability.

steps.title: Read the fixed one-hour example
steps.description: The dashed p=10^-4 curve reaches about 0.63 at 10,000 GPUs. This is the chance of at least one event somewhere, not a fraction of failed devices.

steps.title: Separate better devices from guaranteed correctness
steps.description: The p=10^-5 dotted curve grows more slowly, but increasing fleet size still increases exposure. None of the curves certifies which result is trustworthy after an event.

title: The Robustness Taxonomy
question: Why must the defense match the source of the failure?
scope: The taxonomy names candidate defenses, not universal guarantees; software and pipeline defects cross all three pillars.

steps.title: Identify changed operating data
steps.description: Environmental shifts alter inputs, labels, or their relation. Reweighting, recalibration, and adaptation address different changes and require outcome evidence.

steps.title: Specify the adversary’s access
steps.description: Input-level attacks include evasion, poisoning, and physical perturbations. Their defenses act at different boundaries of data acquisition, training, and serving.

steps.title: Verify the computing substrate
steps.description: System-level faults include silent corruption, bit flips, numerical exceptions, and desynchronization. Input filtering alone does not verify these execution paths.

steps.title: Check the whole pipeline
steps.description: The dashed software boundary spans all pillars. A data or orchestration defect can undermine a defense even when its local method is appropriate.

title: Types of Distribution Shift
question: Which probability changes in each kind of distribution shift?
scope: Panels are schematic regimes; input-only monitoring cannot generally identify label or conditional changes without additional evidence.

steps.title: Move the input population
steps.description: In covariate shift, p(x) changes while p(y|x) is fixed. Training and deployment points occupy different parts of the same decision relationship.

steps.title: Change the class proportions
steps.description: In label shift, p(y) changes while p(x|y) is fixed. The bars compare class priors rather than a new decision boundary.

steps.title: Change the label relationship
steps.description: In concept drift, the old and new boundaries differ: p(y|x) changes, and p(x) may remain fixed. Detecting the changed mapping generally needs outcome evidence.

title: Gradient-Based Attack Geometry
question: Why does the FGSM update land on a corner of the allowed set?
scope: The class boundary and two-dimensional inputs are illustrative; a different gradient or boundary need not yield a successful attack at the same budget.

steps.title: Bound every coordinate change
steps.description: The dashed square contains perturbations whose absolute change in each coordinate is at most epsilon. The budget is coordinate-wise, not the arrow’s Euclidean length.

steps.title: Take the sign of the gradient
steps.description: The short blue arrow gives the local loss gradient. FGSM uses its coordinate signs and applies the full budget to each coordinate.

steps.title: Test the resulting class
steps.description: The red update reaches the upper-left allowed corner. In this particular drawing that corner crosses the decision boundary; the geometry does not guarantee success for every input.

title: Data Poisoning and Interception Workflow
question: Where can an ingestion defense intercept poisoned ratings?
scope: The filter flags suspected records and reduces risk; neither anomaly scores nor the retained rows prove an uncorrupted model.

steps.title: Identify the injected records
steps.description: The red sybil rows assign item 3 a low rating and item 4 a high rating. Their contribution attempts to change recommendation behavior.

steps.title: Trace the unchecked path
steps.description: The upper dashed branch sends contributed records to training without filtering. Its model box illustrates the attacker’s desired suppression and promotion.

steps.title: Separate retained from suspect records
steps.description: The interception stage scores rows and diverts suspected records to quarantine. Legitimate rare data and stealthy poisons can still complicate that decision.

steps.title: Validate before release
steps.description: The filtered path ends at a candidate model, explicitly awaiting validation. A successful ingestion step does not remove the need to evaluate downstream behavior.

title: Autoencoder Ingestion Gate
question: What does reconstruction error establish at an ingestion gate?
scope: The gate is calibrated using held-out clean data; high error is an anomaly signal, not proof of poisoning.

steps.title: Compress the candidate input
steps.description: The encoder maps the input x through progressively narrower layers into latent z. Training on trusted data defines which structures the model learns to reconstruct.

steps.title: Reconstruct the input
steps.description: The decoder expands z into reconstructed x. A well-formed output is not by itself evidence that the record is trusted.

steps.title: Apply the calibrated error threshold
steps.description: The score compares x with its reconstruction. Values at or below tau are accepted; higher values are quarantined. Legitimate unfamiliar inputs can also have high error, so evaluate false rejections and missed poisons.

title: Data Augmentation Techniques
question: When is an image transformation a valid training example?
scope: The visible digit examples illustrate transformations; their label validity and robustness benefit depend on the task and must be evaluated.

steps.title: Fix the intended label
steps.description: The original image depicts a digit 3. An augmented example must preserve the task’s intended answer to remain a valid labeled record.

steps.title: Inspect a potentially invalid flip
steps.description: The mirrored digit changes its orientation. A transformation useful for natural images can violate a digit-recognition label contract.

steps.title: Check retained information after cropping
steps.description: The crop removes part of the source. Whether enough evidence remains for the original class depends on the task.

steps.title: Evaluate rotation rather than assuming benefit
steps.description: Rotation produces another variant, but its label and usefulness require validation. Augmentation is not a general guarantee of poisoning resistance.
